clinicalPearls: Anti-Yo (PCA-1) targets the cerebellar degeneration-related cytoplasmic proteins CDR2 and CDR2L within Purkinje cells.
It occurs almost exclusively in women and is strongly linked to ovarian, fallopian tube, primary peritoneal and breast carcinoma.
Presentation is a subacute, rapidly progressive pancerebellar syndrome with gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, and often nystagmus, oscillopsia and diplopia.
Deficits typically evolve over weeks, then plateau leaving severe fixed disability once Purkinje cells have been lost.
The neurological onset commonly precedes cancer detection, so a positive antibody in a woman warrants dedicated pelvic and breast imaging.
Because CDR2 and CDR2L are intracellular, the disorder responds poorly to immunotherapy and the priority is prompt oncological treatment.
Early MRI is often normal, with cerebellar atrophy appearing only later, so a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis.
Truncal and appendicular ataxia are usually broadly symmetrical and out of proportion to any brainstem signs.
reference.pathophysiology: CDR2 and CDR2L are cytoplasmic proteins normally confined to Purkinje cells, where they interact with transcriptional and cell-cycle regulators. Gynaecological and breast tumours that ectopically express these onconeural antigens provoke an immune response that breaches tolerance. While the anti-Yo antibody is the diagnostic marker, evidence favours antigen-specific cytotoxic T-cell responses, alongside possible antibody internalisation, as the drivers of selective Purkinje cell injury. The result is rapid apoptotic loss of Purkinje neurons with relative early sparing of the granular layer, followed by secondary molecular-layer and dentate degeneration. Because Purkinje cells do not regenerate, once this loss is established the cerebellar deficit becomes fixed, accounting for the characteristic plateau at a severely disabled level.
additionalDifferentials: Other paraneoplastic cerebellar syndromes (anti-Tr/DNER with Hodgkin lymphoma, anti-Hu, anti-Ri, or P/Q-type calcium channel antibodies with Lambert-Eaton syndrome)
Alcohol-related or nutritional (thiamine, vitamin E) cerebellar degeneration
Immune-mediated cerebellar ataxia including anti-GAD and gluten ataxia
Toxic cerebellar injury from phenytoin, lithium or chemotherapy
Rapidly progressive hereditary or sporadic degenerative ataxia
Structural posterior fossa lesion or paraneoplastic brainstem encephalitis
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid anti-Yo (PCA-1) with confirmatory immunohistochemistry and line blot
Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound and CT or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis for ovarian or tubal carcinoma
Whole-body FDG-PET when initial imaging is unrevealing
Serum CA-125 and other tumour markers to support an occult gynaecological malignancy
Cerebrospinal fluid for pleocytosis, raised protein and oligoclonal bands
Serial brain MRI to document evolving cerebellar atrophy
redFlags: Rapidly progressive ataxia rendering a patient unable to walk within weeks
Occult gynaecological or breast malignancy requiring urgent staging and surgery
Dysphagia and dysarthria raising aspiration risk
A positive antibody with negative imaging, prompting consideration of exploratory or risk-reducing surgery
reference.prognosis: The neurological prognosis is poor, with most patients left wheelchair-bound owing to irreversible Purkinje cell loss. Earlier tumour diagnosis and treatment offer the only realistic chance of stabilisation rather than recovery.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because early MRI appears normal
Failing to pursue occult ovarian or breast cancer, including consideration of exploratory or risk-reducing surgery when antibody-positive but imaging-negative
Expecting meaningful recovery from immunotherapy once severe deficits are established
Mislabelling subacute ataxia in a woman as idiopathic or degenerative
Overlooking a second coexisting onconeural antibody
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Consensus diagnostic criteria for paraneoplastic neurological syndromes
management: Tumor control is the primary treatment lever since Yo (PCA-1) targets an intracellular antigen and responds poorly to immunotherapy
Search actively for an underlying ovarian or breast malignancy once the antibody is identified
Treat the underlying tumor with stage-appropriate standard of care such as surgery, systemic therapy, or radiotherapy as indicated by tumor type
Treat the primary tumor in parallel with immune-directed therapy rather than waiting for one before the other
Consider starting empiric treatment without waiting for autoantibody results once high clinical suspicion exists and infection has been reasonably excluded
Use a short course of high-dose corticosteroids as first-line acute immunotherapy
Consider intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange as other first-line options
For non-responders, consider second-line immunosuppressive agents such as rituximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or cyclophosphamide
Expect an overall poor immunotherapy response for Yo-associated disease given its intracellular target and T-cell-mediated mechanism
Consider exploratory or risk-reducing surgery for the underlying malignancy when the antibody is positive but initial imaging is negative
Monitor neurologic status serially for progression of ataxia, recognizing that deficits typically plateau once Purkinje cell loss is established
Monitor with interval imaging and tumor marker surveillance for the primary cancer and recurrence
Monitor for and manage complications of fixed cerebellar disability such as aspiration risk and falls
Refer promptly to gynecologic and breast oncology, neurology or neuroimmunology, and rehabilitation services as the clinical course warrants
